summary: Defines Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST), a simple certificate management protocol for PKI clients that need client certificates and the related CA certificates. It builds on CMC messages sent over a secure transport, and supports keys generated by the client or by the CA.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a safe way for a device to ask for its official ID card and to get the issuer's papers at the same time.

questions: what is est enrollment over secure transport
how to get a certificate over https
how does est server key generation work
subtitle: How a device safely asks a certificate authority for its certificates over HTTPS.

tldr.problem: Devices in a public key infrastructure (PKI) need client certificates and the matching CA certificates, and they need a simple way to get them that does not require a heavy protocol.
tldr.mechanism: EST profiles CMC messages carried over HTTP on top of TLS. A small set of well-known URLs fetch CA certificates, enroll, re-enroll, and optionally run full CMC, have the server generate a key, or list the attributes the CA wants.
tldr.outcome: Clients and servers authenticate each other in the TLS handshake or with HTTP passwords, and the CA decides by local policy whether to issue. RFC 7030 is a Proposed Standard that later RFCs update.

today: RFC 7030 is a Proposed Standard from October 2013 and is updated by RFC 8951, RFC 8996 and RFC 9908. Read it together with those updates.

sections.title: What EST Is For
sections.content:
RFC 7030 defines Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST). It profiles certificate enrollment for clients using Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) messages sent over a secure transport. The goal is a simple but functional protocol for PKI clients that need to acquire client certificates and the associated Certification Authority (CA) certificates.

An EST server sits between a CA and a client and does several jobs that a PKI traditionally gives to a Registration Authority. How the EST server talks to the CA is not described. The RFC defines two extensions beyond CMC: one for requesting Certificate Signing Request (CSR) attributes and one for requesting server-generated keys. It specifies EST over HTTPS, which runs over TCP, and does not specify HTTP over DTLS and UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: A device needs an ID card from the issuing office. EST is the safe, simple way to ask the office for one, using the same secure web connection used for online shopping.

sections.title: Layers: Messages, HTTP and TLS
sections.content:
EST stacks three layers. At the top are the request and response messages. HTTP carries them and signals the operation and result. TLS underneath provides integrity and confidentiality and authenticates the server and, optionally, the client. HTTPS MUST be used, and TLS 1.1 or a later version MUST be used for all EST communications.

Each operation has its own path under the registered name est in the /.well-known/ prefix, for example GET /.well-known/est/cacerts or POST /.well-known/est/simpleenroll. A server MAY serve several CAs by adding an optional label before the operation name. HTTP status codes report success or failure, and the Content-Type header says which kind of message is carried.

Because TLS and HTTP can supply proof of identity, EST uses the CMC Simple PKI message types. Proof of possession, showing that the client holds the private key, is a separate matter, covered by the signed request.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a letter in a locked box. The box is the secure connection, the address on the envelope says what you want, and the letter inside holds the actual request.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
Authentication works in both directions. The EST server MUST be authenticated during the TLS handshake, except when the client is bootstrapping CA certificates or using Full CMC. TLS client authentication with a certificate is the RECOMMENDED way to identify a client, and the EST server MUST support it. HTTP Basic or Digest passwords MAY be used instead or in addition, but only over TLS 1.1 or later, and NULL and anon cipher suites MUST NOT be used.

A third option is a certificate-less TLS cipher suite, where a shared secret authenticates both sides. It MUST be based on a zero knowledge protocol that resists dictionary attack, and TLS-SRP cipher suites are named as suitable.

Both sides also check authorization. The client MUST check that the server is allowed to serve it before accepting responses, using either an Explicit trust anchor database configured for EST or an Implicit one such as the roots web browsers use. The decision to issue a certificate is always controlled by local CA policy.

To bind identity to possession, a client SHOULD embed the TLS tls-unique value, base64 encoded, in the challenge-password field of its request. If included, the server MUST verify it. That field is limited to 255 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides show ID before talking. The device checks it is really talking to the right office, and the office checks the device is allowed to ask. The office alone decides whether to hand out a card.

sections.title: Getting CA Certificates and Enrolling
sections.content:
A client first asks for the CA certificates with an HTTPS GET to /cacerts. A success response is HTTP 200 with a certs-only CMC Simple PKI Response using application/pkcs7-mime. It MUST include the current root CA certificate and any certificates needed to build a chain. A client that has no trust anchors may continue provisionally, but then MUST ask a human to check the CA certificate out of band, for example by a SHA-256 or SHA-512 fingerprint.

To get a certificate, the client sends an HTTPS POST to /simpleenroll with a PKCS #10 request using application/pkcs10. The signature on the CSR provides proof of possession of the private key. To renew or rekey, it posts to /simplereenroll, and the Subject and SubjectAltName MUST match the current certificate. If the public key is unchanged the server renews; if it differs the server rekeys.

A successful response is HTTP 200 containing only the issued certificate. Errors use 4xx or 5xx codes. An HTTP 202 means the request was accepted but is not ready: the server MUST include a Retry-After header and the client MUST wait at least that long before sending the same request again.
sections.plainLanguage: First the device collects the office's official stamps. Then it fills in a form and sends it. The office replies with the new ID card, or says to come back later.

sections.title: Server-Side Key Generation
sections.content:
An EST client MAY ask the server to create the key pair as well, with an HTTPS POST to /serverkeygen. Support is OPTIONAL. The request looks like an enrollment CSR, but the server MUST ignore the public key values and signature in it. Cipher suites with a NULL confidentiality algorithm MUST NOT be used, since they would expose the private key.

A client can ask for extra protection on top of TLS by naming an encryption key in the CSR, either symmetric with a DecryptKeyIdentifier attribute or asymmetric with an AsymmetricDecryptKeyIdentifier attribute. The RFC strongly RECOMMENDS asking for CMS EnvelopedData protection in addition to TLS.

The success response is HTTP 200 with multipart/mixed content in two parts: the private key and the certificate. Without extra encryption the key goes in an application/pkcs8 part. With it, the key is wrapped in CMS and returned as application/pkcs7-mime with smime-type server-generated-key.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the office makes the secret key for you and mails it in a locked pouch, inside the already locked truck. It is allowed, but it is riskier than making your own.

sections.title: Full CMC and CSR Attributes
sections.content:
Two more operations are available. /fullcmc lets a client send a CMC Full PKI Request for functions the simple calls do not offer, such as advanced proof-of-possession methods. Support is OPTIONAL for clients and servers.

/csrattrs lets a client ask, before enrolling, which attributes the CA wants in the request. The server answers with HTTP 200 and an application/csrattrs body, or with 204 or 404 if none are available. The client MUST ignore any attribute it does not recognize. If the CA requires a particular crypto system or signature scheme it MUST say so here, and a server that requires linking identity and proof of possession MUST include the challengePassword OID. The RFC's example asks for a MAC address, the secp384r1 curve and the SHA384 hash.
sections.plainLanguage: Before filling in the form, the device can ask the office what extra details it wants on it. That avoids getting the form sent back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Basic authentication exposes the client's cleartext password to the EST server, so credentials such as a PIN or one-time password should be used only once to obtain a certificate. When a client uses the Implicit trust anchor database, it cannot check that the server is authorized as an RA for its PKI. Such clients are RECOMMENDED to use only TLS client authentication and to link identity and proof of possession, and to disable the Implicit database after the CA certificates are retrieved.

Certificate-less cipher suites must leak only whether a single guess is correct, and the shared secret must not be shared beyond the client and server. Cipher suites with _EXPORT_ or _DES_ in their names MUST NOT be used.

Server-side key generation sends private key material to the client, which is inherently risky. Servers are RECOMMENDED not to support it by default, and clients not to request it without a compelling operational benefit.
sections.plainLanguage: The main danger is trusting the wrong office or letting a secret get seen. So use each password once, and avoid having someone else make your secret key unless you really must.
